## 📘 ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
**Course Code:** 100101

UNIT 1.0- Atomic and Molecular Structure      8 hrs
Electromagnetic radiations, Dual nature of electron and Heisenberg uncertainty Principle.
Photoelectric effect, Planck's theory. Principles for the combination of atomic orbitals to
form a molecular diagram of molecular orbitals. Bent's rule, VSEPR theory (typical
example) co-ordination numbers and geometries. Isomerism in transition metal compounds.
Metal Carbonyls; Synthesis and Structure.
UNIT 2.0- Spectroscopy          6 hrs
Principle of rotational and vibrational spectroscopy, selection rule for application in
diatomic molecules, elementary idea of electronic spectroscopy, UV -VIS spectroscopy with
related to rules and its applications. Basic Principle of nuclear Magnetic resonance
spectroscopy with applications.
UNIT 3.0 -Electrochemistry and Fuels       6 hrs
Nernst equation, EMF and electrochemical cell, the introduction of corrosion, corrosion
mechanism, types of corrosion, water line corrosion, stress corrosion, pitting corrosion,
Lead acid storage cell, leclanche cell. Calorific value of fuels, proximate an d ultimate
analysis of coals, fuel cells, Bio fuels.
UNIT 4.0- Water Chemistry       8 hrs
Hardness of water, estimation of water hardness by EDTA and Alkalinity method. Removal
of the hardness of water - soda lime process, zeolite process, Ion exchange process, Boiler
problem, sludge, and scale formation, priming and foaming, Boiler corrosion, and Caustic
embrittlement.
UNIT 5.0 - Polymer and Plastics       8 hrs
Polymerization techniques (free radical, ionic, and co -ordination mechanism)Preparation
properties, and technical application of phenol -formaldehyde resins, elastomers, synthetic
rubbers (Buna -S, Buna -N, neoprene). Inorganic polymers, Silicones, adhesives, epoxy
resins. the structural difference between thermoplastic and thermosetting Plastics, the
Importance of commercially important thermoplastics and thermosets; Poly ethylene,
Polyvinyl chloride, Polystyrene.
UNIT 6.0- Organic Reactions and Synthesis of A Drug Molecul   6 hrs
Introduction to intermediate and reaction involving Substitution, addition, elimination,
oxidation-reduction. Diels Elder cyclization and epoxide ring opening reactions, synthesis of
commonly used drug molecules like aspirin.
Test/

## 📘 ENGINEERING MATHEMATICS
**Course Code:** 100102

-I   3 1 0 4
### 📌 Unit- 1.0: Linear Algebra-I        7 hrs
Elementary Row operations, Gauss -Jordan Method for finding the inverse of Matrix,
Complex Matrix : Hermitian , Skew Hermitian  and Unitary Matrix, Vector space, Sub
Spaces, Linear dependence and Independences of Vectors, Linear Span, Basis, Dimension,
Extension of basis of subspace, The rank of a matrix, Row and column space, Solvability of
system of linear equations.
### 📌 Unit- 2.0: Linear Algebra-II       7 hrs
Linear Transformations, Kernel and Range of linear transformation, Matrix Representation
of a linear transformation, Rank -Nullity Theorem, Eigen Value and Eigen Vectors,
Properties of Eigen vectors, Eigen Bases, Orthogonal Transformation, Similarity
Transformation, Matrix Diagonalization, Cayley- Hamilton Theorem.
### 📌 Unit- 3.0: Calculus for single variable      7 hrs
Indeterminate form, L'Hospital Rule, Rolle's Theorem, Mean Value Theorem, Expansion of
function (single variable), Taylor and  Maclaurin Series, Riemann Integration, Riemann
Sum, Improper Integrals, Beta and Gamma function and their properties.
### 📌 Unit- 4.0 : Multivariable Calculus (Differentiation)    7 hrs
Function with two or more variable, Limit, continuity and Partial  differentiation, Total
Differentiation
Taylor's series and Maclaurin's series for function with two variable, Jacobian, Maxima and
Minima, Method of Lagrange's multiplier.
### 📌 Unit-5.0: Multivariable Calculus (Integration)     7 hrs
Double Integral, change of  order of integration, Triple integral, Change of Variable in a
Double and Triple Integrals, Change to polar coordinate, Change to cylindrical coordinate,
Change to spherical polar coordinate, Application to area and volume using double and
triple integral
### 📌 Unit- 6.0: Vector Calculus        7 hrs
Scalar and vector fields, Gradient, Directional derivative, Divergence, Curl and their
properties, Line integral, Green's theorem in plane (without proof), Surface integral, Stoke's
theorem (without proof), Volume Integral, Gauss-Divergence' theorem (without proof).
Test/

## 📘 ENGINEERING MECHANICS
**Course Code:** 100105

### 📌 Unit- 1.0:
Fundamentals of Mechanics        7hrs
Overview of engineering mechanics. Vector and scalar quantities. Units of physical
quantities. Dimensions of physical quantities. Units and Dimensions. Dimensional analysis.
### 📌 Unit- 2.0:
Force Systems and Equilibrium       7hrs
Force Systems Basic Concepts, Particle Equilibrium in 2-D & 3-D, Rigid Body Equilibrium,
System of Forces:  Coplanar  Concurrent Forces, Components in Space, Resultant and
Moment of Forces and its Application, Couples and Resultant of Force System, Free Body
Diagrams, Equations of Equilibrium of Coplanar Systems and Spatial Systems.
### 📌 Unit- 3.0:
Friction and Structural Analysis       7hrs
Types of Friction: Limiting, Static, and Dynamic, Laws of Friction, Motion of Bodies and
Wedge Friction, Equilibrium in Three Dimensions, Method of Sections and Method of
Joints, Tension and Compression in Members, Simple Trusses, Zero Fo rce Members,
Beams, Types of Beams, Frames and Machines.
### 📌 Unit- 4.0:
Centroid, Centre of Gravity, and Moment of Inertia    7hrs
Centroid of Simple Figures from First Principle, Centroid of Composite Sections, Centre of
Gravity and Its Implications, Area Moment of Inertia: Definition and Theorems Moment of
Inertia of Plane Sections, Standard Sections, and Composite Sections, Mass Moment Inertia
of Circular Plate, Cylinder, Cone, Sphere, Hook.
### 📌 Unit- 5.0:
Virtual Work, Energy Method, and Particle Dynamics    7hrs
Virtual Displacements and Principle of Virtual Work, Degrees of Freedom and Active Force
Diagram, Conservative Forces and Potential Energy, Energy Equation for Equilibrium,
Applications of Energy Method for Equilibrium, Stability of Equilibrium, Review of
Particle Dynamics: Rectilinear and Plane Curvilinear Motion, Relative and Constrained
Motion, Newton's 2nd Law Work -Kinetic Energy, Power, Potential Energy Impulse -
Momentum and Impact.
### 📌 Unit- 6.0: Kinetics of Rigid Bodies       7hrs
Introduction to Kinetics of Rigid Bodies Basic Terms and General Principles in Dynamics
Types of Motion and Instantaneous Centre of Rotation in Plane Motion Simple Problems
D'Alembert's Principle and Its Applications in Plane Motion and Connected Bodies Work -
Energy Principle  and Its Application in Plane Motion of Connected Bodies Kinetics of
Rigid Body Rotation.
Test/

## 📘 SPORTS/YOGA/NCC/NSS
**Course Code:** 100101P

Course Objectives:
(a) Encouraging creativity and innovation: The course could aim to fos ter a culture of
creativity and innovation among engineering students. It could provide opportu nities for
students to generate and develop new ideas, think critically, and come up with innovative
solutions to real -worldproblems. This objective could be achieved through brainsto rming
sessions, design thinking exercises, and hands-on projects.
(b) Enhancing problem -solving skills: The course could focus on enhancing the problem -
solving skills of engineering students. It could provide training on various problem -solving
techniques, such as r oot cause analysis, critical thinking, and decision -making. Student s
may learn how to identify and analyse complex problems, develop feasible solutions, and
implement them effectively.
(c) Developing project management skills: The cour se could aim to devel op project
management skills among engineering students. It cou ld cover topics such as project
planning, scheduling, budgeting, and risk management. Students may learn how to manage
resources, communicate effectively, and work collaboratively in a project -based
environment.
(d) Promoting interdisciplinary collaboration: The course could encourage interdisciplinary
collaboration among engineering students. It could provide opportunities for students from
different engineering disciplines to work together on innovative pro jects. This could foster
cross-disciplinary learning, encourage diverse perspectives, and promo te teamwork and
collaboration skills.
(e) Facilitating practical application of engineering concepts: The course could focus on the
practical application of engineering concepts and principles. It could provide students with
opportunities to apply their theoretical knowledge to real-world projects, prototypes, or
simulations. Students may learn how to translate engineering theories into practical
solutions and develop hands-on experience in implementing innovative projects.
Pre-requisite: Nil
Course Outcome:

#### 1. Developed innovative projects: Students may have su ccessfully developed innovative
projects that demonstrate their creativity, problem -solving skills, and technical competence.
These projects could be prototypes, models, simulations, or practical sol utions to real-world
problems, showcasing their ability to apply engineering concepts in a creative an d
innovative manner.

#### 2. Improved critical thinking and problem -solving skills: Student s may have honed their
critical thinking and problem -solving skills through various course activities , such as
brainstorming, design thinking, and project development. They may have learned to analyse
complex problems, identify viable solutions, and make informed decisions based on
technical, economic, and social considerations.

#### 3. Enhanced project management and teamwork skills: Students may have gained practical
experience in managing projects, including planning, scheduling, budgeting, and risk
management. They may have learned how to work effectively in a team, collabor ate with
diverse team members, and communicate project progress and results professionally.

#### 4. Increased interdisciplinary knowledge and collaboration: Students may have gained
exposure to interdisciplinary concepts and collaborated with peers from different
engineering disciplines. They may have learned to appreciate diverse perspectives, leverage
interdisciplinary knowledge, and work collaboratively to develop innovative solutions that
integrate multiple domains of engineering.

#### 5. Cultivated a mindset of innovation and entrepreneurship: Students may have developed a
mindset of  innovation and entrepreneurship, recognizing the importance of creativity,
adaptability, and continuous improvement in engineering practice. They may have learned
to identify opportunities, think critically, and take risks to develop and implement
innovative projects with commercial or societal potential.
List of Reports:
Any topics related to innovative project.

## 📘 ENGINEERING PHYSICS
**Course Code:** 100110

### 📌 Unit- 1.0

#### 1. Frame of Reference
:         2 hrs
Non-Inertial frame of reference, rotating coordinate system, centripetal and Coriolis
acceleration and its application in weather system.

#### 2. Oscillations:          3 hrs
Harmonic Oscillator, Damped Harmonic motion - overdamped, critically  Damped and
lightly damped oscillators, Force Oscillators and Resonance.
### 📌 Unit- 2.0

#### 1. Optics
:           4 hrs
Huygens's Principle, Superposition of Waves and interference of Light by wave front -
splitting and amplitude-splitting; Young's double slit experiment, Michelson interferometer,
Fraunhofer diffraction from single slit and circular aperture, Diffract ion Grating and their
resolving power

#### 2. LASER:           4 hrs
Einstein's theory of matter -radiations interaction, Einstein's Coefficients (A and B),
Amplification by population inversion, Different types of lasers - Gas Laser, Helium-Neon
Laser, Solid State Laser (Ruby, Neodymium), Semiconductor Laser.
### 📌 Unit- 3.0

#### 1. Quantum Mechanics
:        5 hrs
Compton Effect, Photoelectric Effect, Wave Particle duality, de Broglie's hypothesis,
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, Wave function and wave packets, phase and group
velocities, Schrodinger's Wave Equation, Normalization, Expectation values, Eigenvalue s
and Eigenfunction.

#### 2. Applications in One dimensions:       2 hrs
Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box - its
wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and momentum.
### 📌 Unit- 4.0

#### 1. Vector Calculus
:          2 hrs
Gradient, Divergence and Curl, Line, Surface and Volume integrals, Gauss's Divergence
theorem and Stokes' theorem in Cartesian Coordinate.

#### 2. Electrostatics:         4 hrs
Gauss's Law and its applications, Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic fields, Electrostat ic
Potential, Boundary Conditions, Poisson's and Laplace's equations, Dielectrics,
Polarization, Bound Charges, Electric displacement, Boundary Conditions in dielectrics.
### 📌 Unit- 5.0

#### 1. Magnetostatics
:          4 hrs
Lorentz force, Biot -Savart and Ampere's circuital laws and their applications, Divergence
and Curl of Magneto static fields, Magnetic vector potential, Force and torque on a magnetic
dipole, Magnetic Materials, Magnetization, Bound currents, Boundary conditions.

#### 2. Electrodynamics and Electromagnetic Waves:     4 hrs
Ohm's law, Motional EMF, Faraday's Law, Lenz's law, Self and mutual inductance, Energy
stored in magnetic field, Maxwell's equations in vacuum and nonconducting medium,
Continuity Equation, Poynting Theorem, Wave Equations: plain ele ctromagnetic wave in
vacuum and their transverse nature and Polarization.
### 📌 Unit- 6.0

#### 1. Introduction to Solids and Semi-Conductors
:      3 hrs
Free electron theory of metal, fermi level, Bloch's theorem for particle in a periodic
Potential, Kroning-Penney model and origin of energy band.

#### 2. Electronic Materials:         3 hrs
Metals, semiconductors and insulators, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors,Carrier
transport, diffusion and drift, P-N junction.
Test/

## 📘 PROGRAMMING FOR PROBLEM SOLVING
**Course Code:** 100111

### 📌 Unit- 1.0: Introduction to Programming        6 hrs
Introduction to Programming        6 hrs
Introduction to components of a computer system (disks, memory, processor, where a
program is stored and executed, operating system, compilers etc.). Idea of Algorithm: steps
to solve logical and numerical problems. Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/  Pseudo
code with examples. From algorithms to programs; source code, variables (with data types)
variables and memory locations, Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation, object and
executable code.
### 📌 Unit- 2.0: Operators, Conditional Branching and Loops     8 hrs
Operators, Conditional Branching and Loops     8 hrs
Arithmetic expressions/arithmetic operators, relational operators, logical operators, bitwise
operators and precedence. Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching,
Iteration and loops.
### 📌 Unit- 3.0: Arrays and String         6 hrs
Arrays and String         6 hrs
Array declaration & initialization, bo und checking arrays (1 -d, 2 -d), character arrays and
strings.
### 📌 Unit- 4.0: Function, Recursion and Pointers       9 hrs
Function, Recursion and Pointers       9 hrs
Functions (including using built in libraries), Parameter passing in functions , call by value,
passing arrays to functions: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems. Example
programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc. Idea of
pointers, Defining pointers, Use of Pointers in self - referential structures, idea of call by
reference.
### 📌 Unit- 5.0: User defined Data Types and File handling          8
User defined Data Types and File handling          8 hrs
Structure- defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of
structure, array of structures, structures within structure , structure and function, type
definition; Union - definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union.
Introduction, file declaration, opening and closing a file, working with text and binary files,
I/O operations on file, error handling, random access to files
### 📌 Unit- 6.0: Basic Algorithms         5 hrs
Basic Algorithms         5 hrs
Searching, Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection), Finding roots of
equations, notion of order of complexity through  example programs (no formal definition
required)

:          4 hrs

stored in magnetic field, Maxwell's equations in vacuum and nonconducting medium,
Continuity Equation, Poynting Theorem, Wave Equati ons: plain electromagnetic wave in
vacuum and their transverse nature and Polarization.

## Structural Design-I
**Course Code:** 101501
3 1 0 4

#### Unit-1.0: Fundamentals of RC Design and the Working Stress Method
6 hrs
Fundamentals of RC Design and the Working Stress Method:
This unit introduces the basic material properties of concrete and steel, and the foundational
design concepts using the elastic theory. It covers the traditional working stress method
(WSM) and its application to different types of beam sections.
Concepts of Reinforced Concrete: Introduction to RC, stress-strain characteristics of
concrete and steel, and the elastic theory.
Working Stress Method: Design philosophy and assumptions of the method.
Singly Reinforced Beam Analysis and Design: Analysis and design of balanced, under-
reinforced, and over-reinforced rectangular sections using the WSM.

#### Unit-2.0: Limit State Method
9 hrs
Limit State Method: Principles and Design of Beams:
This unit transitions to the modern limit state method (LSM) of design. It explains the core
concepts of LSM and applies them to the design of various beam types for flexure, shear, and
torsion.
Concepts of Limit State Method: Principles of probability and reliability, characteristic
loads and strengths, partial safety factors for loads and materials, and the different limit states
of collapse and serviceability.
Design of Beams for Flexure: Design of singly reinforced, doubly reinforced, rectangular,
and T-sections.
Design for Shear and Bond: Principles of shear resistance, design of shear reinforcement,
and ensuring proper bond and anchorage.
Design for Bending and Torsion: Design of beams subjected to combined bending and
torsion as per IS Code recommendations.

#### Unit-3.0: Design of Compression Members (Columns)
7 hrs
Design of Compression Members (Columns):
This unit focuses on the design of columns, which are critical elements for supporting axial
and bending loads. It covers short and slender columns under various loading conditions.
Design for Axial Loads: Design of short columns subjected to direct compression.
Design for Uni-axial Bending: Design of columns subjected to combined axial load and uni-
axial bending moment as per IS Code methods.
Design for Bi-axial Bending: Design of columns for axial load and bi-axial bending
moment.
B.Tech (Civil Engineering)
(SESSION 2024 onwards)

#### Unit-4.0: Design of Slabs and Staircases
6 hrs
Design of Slabs and Staircases:
This unit covers the design of common slab systems and different types of staircases. It
includes the design of one-way and two-way slabs, as well as complex slab systems like flat
slabs.
Design of Slabs: Design of one-way and two-way slabs.
Design of Flat Slabs: Design considerations for flat slabs.
Design of Staircases: Design of dog-legged and open-well type staircases.

#### Unit-5.0:
6 hrs
Design of Foundations:
This unit addresses the design of various types of concrete foundations for transferring
building loads to the supporting soil.
Design of Isolated Footings: Design of square and rectangular isolated footings subjected to
axial load and moments.
Design of Combined Foundations: Design of combined footings for supporting multiple
columns.

#### Unit-6.0: Prestressed Concrete
8 hrs
Prestressed Concrete:
This unit introduces the advanced topic of prestressed concrete. It covers the fundamental
principles, materials, prestressing methods, and the analysis of prestressed members.
Principles of Prestressed Concrete: Basic principles, materials, and methods of prestressing
(pre-tensioning and post-tensioning).
Losses in Prestress: Analysis of various types of losses, including elastic shortening, creep,
shrinkage, and friction.
Analysis of Prestressed Sections: Analysis of various types of sections (rectangular, T-
section, box section, and girders) subjected to prestress and external loads.
Design of Slabs: Design of post-tensioned slabs.

**Course Code:** 102501

#### Unit-1.0: Introduction

Three modes of heat transfer; Examples of equipment (like air conditioner and air cooler) involving heat
transfer; Derivation of heat balance equation.

#### Unit-2.0: Conduction Heat Transfer
7 hrs

forced and free convection; Approximate solutions to laminar boundary layer equations for internal and
external flow; Estimating heat transfer rates in laminar and turbulent flow situations using appropriate
correlations for free and forced convection.

7 hrs

Black and grey body radiation; Calculation of radiation heat transfer between surfaces using radiative
properties; View factors and the radiosity method; Examples for two-body enclosures; Radiation shield.

#### Unit-5.0: Heat Exchanger Design
7 hrs

difference; Heat exchanger effectiveness; Analysis, design and selection of heat exchangers.

#### Unit-6.0:
7 hrs
Boiling and Condensation heat transfer
Pool boiling; Flow boiling; Film and drop wise condensation.
Introduction to mass transfer
Analogy between heat and mass transfer; Mass diffusion; Fick’s Law; Steady and transient mass
diffusion; Simultaneous heat and mass transfer.

## Power System-I

#### Unit-1.0: Introduction to Power System
6 hrs
Introduction to Power System, Introduction to Conventional and Renewable Energy Sources,Single Line
Diagram, Per-Unit representation of Power system– Selection of base quantities, percent and per unit values,
advantage of per unit system

#### Unit-2.0: Transmission line parameters
10 hrs
Resistance, Inductance, Capacitance, and Conductance. Inductance of single-phase line, inductance of
three-phase line with symmetrical and unsymmetrical spacing, concept of GMD and GMR. Inductance of
composite conductor systems – stranded conductors, bundle conductors, and Double circuit lines.
Capacitance of single-phase line, capacitance of three-phase lines with symmetrical and unsymmetrical
spacings, capacitance calculation for double circuit line and bundle conductor. Effect of the Earth on
capacitance calculation. Skin effect, proximity effect, and Ferranti effect. Interference between power and
communication lines.

#### Unit -3.0: Line Representation
6 hrs
Representation of short, medium, and long lines, Pi and T models. ABCD constant of transmission lines
and their measurement. Travelling wave interpretation of long line equations, tuned lines.

#### Unit -4.0: Transmission line structure
8 hrs
Types of conductors, line supports – poles, towers, stay, & Guy wires, Sag and Tension calculations,
stringing chart, sag template. Insulators – Materials of insulators, types of insulators – Pin and Disc type –
their applications. Underground Cables – Construction of cables, single and multicore cables, different
types, capacitance of belted cables, dielectric loss in cables, heating of cables.

#### Unit -5.0: Aspects of Electrical Supply
6 hrs
Legal aspects of electricity supply- Electricity acts, rules, and codes. Standards followed in power supply,
environmental, and safety measures Commercial aspects of electricity supply – Expenditure in the power
Utility. Factors influencing tariffs, types of consumers, and different types of tariffs. Administrative
aspects of electricity supply- Development of power sector in India. Administrative set up and
organisations in the power sector.

#### Unit -6.0: HVDC Transmission
6 hrs
Comparison of AC and DC Transmission (Economics, Technical Performance and Reliability).
Application of DC Transmission. Types of HVDC Systems. Components of an HV DC system. Line
Commutated Converter and Voltage Source Converter-based systems

9 hrs
Standard test signals. Time response of first and second order systems for standard test inputs. Application

Lead and Lag compensation in designs. Analog and Digital implementation of controllers.

## POWER SYSTEMS - II (OPERATION AND CONTROL)

#### Course Outcomes

*   Use numerical methods to analyse a power system in steady state.
*   Understand stability constraints in a synchronous grid.
*   Understand methods to control the voltage, frequency and power flow.
*   Understand the monitoring and control of a power system.
*   Understand the basics of power system economics.

#### Module 1: Power Flow Analysis 

Review of the structure of a Power System and its components. Analysis of Power Flows: Formation of Bus Admittance Matrix. Real and reactive power balance equations at a node. Load and Generator Specifications. Application of numerical methods for solution of non-linear algebraic equations: Gauss-Seidel and Newton-Raphson methods for the solution of the power flow equations. Computational issues in large-scale power systems.

#### Module 2: Stability Constraints in Synchronous Grids 

Swing Equations of a synchronous machine connected to an infinite bus. Power angle curve. Description of the phenomena of loss of synchronism in a single-machine infinite bus system following a disturbance like a three-phase fault. Analysis using numerical integration of swing equations (Forward Euler, Runge-Kutta 4th order methods) and the Equal Area Criterion. Impact of stability constraints on power system operation. Effect of generation rescheduling and series compensation of transmission lines on stability.

#### Module 3: Control of Frequency and Voltage 

Turbines and Speed-Governors, frequency dependence of loads, Droop Control and Power Sharing. Automatic Generation Control. Generation and absorption of reactive power by various components of a Power System. Excitation System Control in synchronous generators, Automatic Voltage Regulators. Shunt Compensators, Static VAR Compensators and STATCOMs. Tap Changing Transformers. Power flow control using embedded DC links and phase shifters.

#### Module 4: Monitoring and Control 

Overview of Energy Control Centre Functions: SCADA systems. Phasor Measurement Units and Wide-Area Measurement Systems. State-estimation. System Security Assessment. Normal, Alert, Emergency, Extremis states of a power system. Contingency Analysis. Preventive Control and Emergency Control.

#### Module 5: Fault Analysis and Protection Systems 

Method of Symmetrical Components (positive, negative, and zero sequences). Balanced and unbalanced faults. Representation of generators, lines, and transformers in sequence networks. Computation of fault currents. Neutral Grounding.

## "ELECTIVE- 1 & 2" ELECTRICAL DRIVES

#### Module 1: DC Motor Characteristics

DC Motor Characteristics: Review of emf and torque equations of DC machine, review of torque-speed characteristics of separately excited dc motor, change in torque-speed curve with armature voltage, example load torque-speed characteristics, operating point, armature voltage control for varying motor speed, flux weakening for high speed operation.

#### Module 2: Chopper Fed DC Drive

Chopper Fed DC Drive: Review of dc chopper and duty ratio control, chopper fed dc motor for speed control, steady state operation of a chopper fed drive, armature current waveform and ripple, calculation of losses in dc motor and chopper, efficiency of dc drive, smooth starting.

#### Module 3: Multi

Multi-Quadrant DC Drive: Review of motoring and generating modes operation of a separately excited dc machine, four quadrant operation of dc machine; single-quadrant, two-quadrant and four-quadrant choppers; steady-state operation of multi-quadrant chopper fed dc drive, regenerative braking.

#### Module 4: Closed

Closed-Loop Control of DC Drive: Control structure of DC drive, inner current loop and outer speed loop, dynamic model of dc motor dynamic equations and transfer functions, modeling of chopper as gain with switching delay, plant transfer function, for controller design, current controller specification and design, speed controller specification and design.

#### Module 5: Induction Motor Characteristics

Induction Motor Characteristics: Review of induction motor equivalent circuit and torque-speed characteristic, variation of torque-speed curve with (i) applied voltage, (ii) applied frequency and (iii) applied voltage and frequency, typical torque-speed curves of fan and pump loads, operating point, constant flux operation, flux weakening operation.

#### Module 6: Scalar Control or Constant V/f Control of Induction Motor

Scalar Control or Constant V/f Control of Induction Motor: Review of three-phase voltage source inverter, generation of three-phase PWM signals, sinusoidal modulation, space vector theory, conventional space vector modulation; constant V/f control of induction motor, steady-state performance analysis based on equivalent circuit, speed drop with loading, slip regulation.

#### Module 7: Control of Slip Ring Induction Motor

Control of Slip Ring Induction Motor: Impact of rotor resistance of the induction motor torque-speed curve, operation of slip-ring induction motor with external rotor resistance, starting torque, power electronic based rotor side control of slip ring motor, slip power recovery.

## NPTEL-II (Core Courses)
**Course Code:** 110605
12 Weeks (3 Credits)
NPTEL (Core Course) Guidelines:
NPTEL (Core Course) should be taken from the core subjects of the branch.

## DIGITAL COMMUNICATION

#### 1\. Introduction 

*   Block Diagram of Digital Communication System.
*   Advantages over Analog Communication Systems.
*   Sampling theorem, Signal reconstruction in time domain.
*   Practical and Flat Top Sampling.
*   Sampling of Band-pass Signal, Aliasing Problem.
*   Uniform and Non-uniform quantization.
*   Signal to Quantization ratio of Quantized Signal.

#### 2\. Baseband Transmission 

*   Line Coding and its properties.
*   Various types of PCM waveforms and their attributes.
*   Mary Pulse Modulation waveforms.
*   Differential Pulse Code Modulation (DPCM).
*   Multiplexing of PCM signals.
*   Delta modulation, Idling noise and slope overload.
*   Adaptive Delta Modulation, Adaptive DPCM.
*   Comparison of PCM and DM.

#### 3\. Baseband Detection 

*   Error performance degradation in communication systems, Eb/N0 parameter.
*   Matched filter and its derivation.
*   Inter-Symbol Interference (ISI), Nyquist criterion for zero ISI, Raised cosine spectrum.
*   Correlation detector: Decision threshold and Error probability for Binary, Unipolar (on-off) signalling.

#### 4\. Band-pass Modulation and Demodulation 

*   Types of digital modulation.
*   Waveforms for Amplitude, Frequency and Phase Shift Keying.
*   Generation and detection of coherent and non-coherent binary ASK, FSK, PSK.
*   Differential phase shift keying, Quadrature modulation techniques.
*   M-ary FSK, Minimum Shift Keying (MSK).
*   Probability of error and comparison of various digital modulation techniques.

#### 5\. Error 

*   Baseband signal receiver, Probability of error, The Optimum filter, Matched Filter.
*   Coherent reception: ASK, PSK, FSK.
*   Non-Coherent reception: ASK, FSK, PSK, QPSK.
*   Calculation of bit error probability of BPSK and BFSK.
*   Error probability for QPSK.

#### 6\. Multiple Access Techniques 

*   Time Division Multiplexing (TDM).
*   Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM).
*   Code Division Multiplexing (CDM).
*   Introduction to upcoming techniques of transmission.

## ELECTRONICS INSTRUMENTS AND MEASUREMENTS

#### 1\. Introduction 

*   Standards of Measurement.
*   Errors and their evaluation.
*   Calibration, Accuracy, Precision, Sensitivity, Resolution, Noise, etc.

#### 2\. Measurements of Voltage, Current, Power and Energy 

*   Moving iron, moving coil, thermal, induction and rectifier type instruments.
*   Measurements of power factor and frequency: Dynamometer and moving iron single and three-phase power factor meters, resonance, moving coil and moving iron frequency meters.
*   Range extension of voltmeter, ammeter, wattmeter and energy meter: Voltmeter multipliers, ammeter shunt, current and potential transformers.

#### 3\. Galvanometer 

*   D'Arsonval, Vibration and Ballistic galvanometers.

#### 4\. Bridges 

*   D.C. bridges: Kelvin double bridge, Wheatstone bridge, Carey-Foster bridge.
*   A.C. bridges: Maxwell Bridge, Hay and Owen bridges, Anderson Bridge, Wien Bridge, Schering Bridge, Heaviside-Campbell Bridge.

#### 5\. Potentiometers 

*   Principle, Standardization and applications.
*   D.C. Potentiometers: Crompton and Vernier potentiometers.
*   A.C. Potentiometers: Coordinate type and Polar type.

#### 6\. Magnetic Measurements 

*   Measurement of magnetic flux by ballistic galvanometer and fluxmeter.
*   Determination of B-H curve and hysteresis loop.
*   Separation of iron loss into hysteresis and eddy current losses.
*   Measurement of iron loss and its separation using Lloyd-Fisher squares.

#### 7\. Digital Measurements 

*   Digital voltmeter and multimeter.
*   Universal counter and its uses for measurement of frequency, ratio of two frequencies, time period and pulse width.

## COMPUTER ORGANISATION AND ARCHITECTURE

#### 1\. Introduction 

*   Computer Arithmetic, Instruction sets.
*   Introduction to computer organization, CPU Design.
*   Microprogrammed Control: Control Memory, Address sequencing, Microprogramming, sequencing and execution of microinstructions.

#### 2\. Memory System 

*   Hierarchical memory structure, Cache memories, Set Associative memory.
*   Virtual Memory, Paging, Segmentation.
*   Input-Output Interface: Asynchronous Data Transfer, Programmed I/O, Interrupts, Direct Memory Access (DMA).

#### 3\. Input-Output Organization 

*   Basic Input/Output Structure of Computers.
*   Serial and parallel communications, Asynchronous Data Communication.
*   Programmed I/O, Interrupt Driven I/O, Interrupt Controller, DMA, Device Drivers, Buses.

#### 4\. Introduction to Parallel Processing 

*   Evolution of computer systems (RISC vs. CISC).
*   Parallelism in uniprocessor systems.
*   Architectural classification schemes.

#### 5\. Principles of Pipelining and Vector Processing 

*   Pipeline strategy, Pipeline performance, Controls and Data paths.
*   Overlapped parallelism, Principles of designing pipelined processors.
*   Vector processing requirements.

## Structural Design-I
**Course Code:** 101501
3 1 0 4

#### Unit-1.0: Fundamentals of RC Design and the Working Stress Method
6 hrs
Fundamentals of RC Design and the Working Stress Method:
This unit introduces the basic material properties of concrete and steel, and the foundational
design concepts using the elastic theory. It covers the traditional working stress method
(WSM) and its application to different types of beam sections.
Concepts of Reinforced Concrete: Introduction to RC, stress-strain characteristics of
concrete and steel, and the elastic theory.
Working Stress Method: Design philosophy and assumptions of the method.
Singly Reinforced Beam Analysis and Design: Analysis and design of balanced, under-
reinforced, and over-reinforced rectangular sections using the WSM.

#### Unit-2.0: Limit State Method
9 hrs
Limit State Method: Principles and Design of Beams:
This unit transitions to the modern limit state method (LSM) of design. It explains the core
concepts of LSM and applies them to the design of various beam types for flexure, shear, and
torsion.
Concepts of Limit State Method: Principles of probability and reliability, characteristic
loads and strengths, partial safety factors for loads and materials, and the different limit states
of collapse and serviceability.
Design of Beams for Flexure: Design of singly reinforced, doubly reinforced, rectangular,
and T-sections.
Design for Shear and Bond: Principles of shear resistance, design of shear reinforcement,
and ensuring proper bond and anchorage.
Design for Bending and Torsion: Design of beams subjected to combined bending and
torsion as per IS Code recommendations.

#### Unit-3.0: Design of Compression Members (Columns)
7 hrs
Design of Compression Members (Columns):
This unit focuses on the design of columns, which are critical elements for supporting axial
and bending loads. It covers short and slender columns under various loading conditions.
Design for Axial Loads: Design of short columns subjected to direct compression.
Design for Uni-axial Bending: Design of columns subjected to combined axial load and uni-
axial bending moment as per IS Code methods.
Design for Bi-axial Bending: Design of columns for axial load and bi-axial bending
moment.

#### Unit-4.0: Design of Slabs and Staircases
6 hrs
Design of Slabs and Staircases:
This unit covers the design of common slab systems and different types of staircases. It
includes the design of one-way and two-way slabs, as well as complex slab systems like flat
slabs.
Design of Slabs: Design of one-way and two-way slabs.
Design of Flat Slabs: Design considerations for flat slabs.
Design of Staircases: Design of dog-legged and open-well type staircases.

#### Unit-5.0:
6 hrs
Design of Foundations:
This unit addresses the design of various types of concrete foundations for transferring
building loads to the supporting soil.
Design of Isolated Footings: Design of square and rectangular isolated footings subjected to
axial load and moments.
B.Tech (Civil Engineering with CA)
(SESSION 2024 Onwards)
Design of Combined Foundations: Design of combined footings for supporting multiple
columns.

#### Unit-6.0: Prestressed Concrete
8 hrs
Prestressed Concrete:
This unit introduces the advanced topic of prestressed concrete. It covers the fundamental
principles, materials, prestressing methods, and the analysis of prestressed members.
Principles of Prestressed Concrete: Basic principles, materials, and methods of prestressing
(pre-tensioning and post-tensioning).
Losses in Prestress: Analysis of various types of losses, including elastic shortening, creep,
shrinkage, and friction.
Analysis of Prestressed Sections: Analysis of various types of sections (rectangular, T-
section, box section, and girders) subjected to prestress and external loads.
Design of Slabs: Design of post-tensioned slabs.

## Introduction to Finite Element analysis
**Course Code-**
Introduction to Finite Element analysis
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction and Fundamental Concepts
7 hrs
Introduction to FEM: Engineering applications, advantages over other methods, general
steps of the finite element method (discretization, element types, assembly, boundary
conditions, solution, post-processing).
Basic Equations of Solid Mechanics: Review of stress and equilibrium, strain-displacement
relations, and stress-strain relations (Hooke's law) for 1D, 2D (plane stress/strain), and 3D
cases.
Mathematical Formulations: Introduction to numerical methods, potential energy method,
principle of virtual work, and the Galerkin method (weighted residuals approach) for deriving
element equations.

#### Unit- 2.0 One-Dimensional Problems and Structural Elements
7 hrs
1D Problem Formulation: Finite element modeling, local and global coordinate systems,
shape functions (linear and quadratic).
Element Stiffness and Load Vector: Derivation of stiffness matrices and load vectors using
the potential energy approach.
Assembly and Boundary Conditions: Assembly of global stiffness matrix and load vector,
and techniques for handling boundary conditions (elimination method and penalty method).
Analysis of Trusses and Beams: Formulation of element matrices for plane truss and beam
elements, assembly of global matrices, and solution for displacements, reactions, and stresses.

#### Unit- 3.0 Two-Dimensional Stress Analysis
7 hrs
Plane Stress and Plane Strain: Basic concepts and applicability.
Constant Strain Triangles (CST): Derivation of stiffness matrix for 2D triangular elements,
stress and strain calculations (constant within the element).
Axi-Symmetric Problems: Finite element modeling of axi-symmetric solids subjected to
axi-symmetric loading using triangular elements.

#### Unit- 4.0 Isoparametric Formulation and Numerical Integration
7 hrs
Isoparametric Elements: Concepts of isoparametric, subparametric, and superparametric
elements.
Shape Functions: Derivation of shape functions for 2D four-noded quadrilateral isoparametric
elements (linear and serendipity elements).
Numerical Integration: Introduction to numerical integration techniques, specifically Gauss
quadrature for evaluating element stiffness matrices and load vectors for higher-order and
isoparametric elements.

#### Unit- 5.0 Application to Field Problems and Heat Transfer
7 hrs
Heat Transfer Analysis: Formulation and application of FEM to steady-state heat transfer
problems.
1D and 2D Applications: One-dimensional analysis of composite walls and fins; two-
dimensional analysis of thin plates.
Other Field Problems: Introduction to application of FEM in fluid mechanics and
electromagnetics (overview).

#### Unit- 6.0 Dynamic Analysis and Software Applications
7 hrs
Dynamic Analysis Fundamentals: Formulation of finite element models for dynamic
problems, concept of mass matrices (lumped and consistent).
Eigenvalue Problems: Evaluation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors for simple stepped bars
and beams to determine natural frequencies.
Software Applications: Introduction to commercial FEA packages (e.g., ANSYS,
ABAQUS, Nastran) and their usage in pre-processing (mesh generation), solving, and post-
processing (result interpretation).

content, detailed, and bid estimates.

definition to final cost presentation.

## Environmental Fluid Mechanics
**Course Code-**
Environmental Fluid Mechanics
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Fundamentals of Fluid Motion and Conservation Principles
7 hrs
This unit introduces basic concepts and the primary governing equations for fluid flow.
Fluid Properties: Distinction between fluid and solid, density, specific weight, specific
gravity, viscosity (dynamic and kinematic), vapor pressure, surface tension, and
compressibility.
Flow Kinematics: Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions, flow visualization techniques
(streamlines, pathlines, streaklines, time-lines), acceleration of fluid particles, rotation,
vorticity, and circulation.
Conservation Equations: Derivation of the control volume and differential forms of the
continuity equation (mass conservation), momentum equation (Navier-Stokes equations for
incompressible fluids), and energy equation.
Engineering Applications: Application of the Bernoulli and momentum equations to
practical problems in civil engineering.

#### Unit- 2.0 Potential Flow and Ideal Fluid Dynamics
7 hrs
This unit covers ideal, inviscid flow scenarios, which provide foundational solutions for more
complex flows.
Inviscid Flow: Euler's equations of motion, concept of velocity potential and stream function for 2D
flows.
Potential Flow Theory: Laplace's equation for potential flow, simple flow patterns (uniform flow,
source, sink, vortex, doublet), and the superposition of these patterns to form flow nets.
Flow Past Objects: Pressure distribution and force calculations (lift and drag) on immersed bodies
using potential flow theory and conformal transformations.

#### Unit- 3.0 Viscous Laminar Flow
7 hrs
This unit focuses on flows where viscous forces are dominant and fluid motion is orderly.
Navier-Stokes Solutions: Exact solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations for simple geometries.
Internal Flows: Fully developed laminar flow in pipes (Hagen-Poiseuille flow) and between parallel
plates (Couette flow).
Creeping Flow: Introduction to Stokes' law for very low Reynolds number flows.

#### Unit- 4.0 Turbulence
7 hrs
This unit explores the nature and modeling of turbulent flows, which are prevalent in natural
environmental systems.
Introduction to Turbulence: Characteristics of turbulent flow, Reynolds number criteria, and the
difference between laminar and turbulent regimes.
Turbulence Modeling: Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations, mixing length
hypothesis, and basic closure schemes.
Environmental Context: Discussion on the role of turbulence in mixing and dispersion of
contaminants in air and water systems.

#### Unit- 5.0 Boundary Layer Theory
7 hrs
This unit details the region near solid boundaries where viscous effects are significant, a crucial
concept for civil engineering designs.
Boundary Layer Formation: Development of laminar and turbulent boundary layers over
flat plates.
Governing Equations: Boundary layer approximations and order-of-magnitude analysis.
Analysis: Von Kármán momentum integral equation, skin friction drag, and flow separation.

#### Unit- 6.0 Environmental Applications and Transport Processes
7 hrs
This unit integrates the fundamental principles into real-world civil engineering and
environmental scenarios.
Open Channel Flow: Hydraulic characteristics, uniform flow (Manning's equation),
gradually varied flow, and the hydraulic jump.
Environmental Transport: Advective and diffusive transport mechanisms, the advection-
diffusion equation, and dispersion in rivers, lakes, and porous media (groundwater).

## Steel Concrete Composite structures
**Course Code-**
Steel Concrete Composite structures
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction and Fundamental Behaviour
7 hrs
Introduction to Composite Construction: Historical background, advantages and
disadvantages, applications in buildings and bridges, role of different components (steel
beam, concrete slab, shear connectors).
Codes of Practice: Overview of relevant design codes (e.g., Eurocode 4, IS 11384, AISC
specifications).
Composite Action: Concept of full and partial shear interaction, basic theory of composite
beams, stress distribution at the interface.
Construction and Serviceability Issues: Erection sequence, propped vs. unpropped
construction, deflection, vibration, and cracking considerations.

#### Unit- 2.0 Design of Composite Beams and Slabs
7 hrs
Composite Slabs: Behaviour of concrete slabs with profiled steel decking, design for flexure,
shear, and vertical shear resistance, fire resistance.
Composite Beams: Design methods (e.g., Limit State Method, Plastic theory for compact
sections), effective width of concrete flange, shear lag effect.
Flexural and Shear Capacity: Calculation of moment of resistance and shear resistance,
design for longitudinal shear.

#### Unit- 3.0 Design of Shear Connectors and Connections
7 hrs
Shear Connectors: Types of shear connectors (headed studs, channels, etc.), behavior, and
testing methods.
Design of Shear Connectors: Determination of shear capacity for individual connectors,
spacing requirements, partial shear interaction design principles.
Connections in Composite Structures: Design of beam-to-column connections, column bases,
and other critical joints.

#### Unit- 4.0 Design of Composite Columns and Frames
7 hrs
Composite Columns: Behavior of concrete-encased steel sections and concrete-filled steel
tubes (CFST), load-carrying mechanisms, local buckling considerations.
Design for Axial Load and Bending: Interaction curves for axial load and moment, effective
length of columns, design for slender columns.
Composite Frames: Introduction to the behavior and analysis of composite frames, design
concepts for multi-storey buildings.

#### Unit- 5.0 Composite Box Girders and Bridges
7 hrs
Introduction to Composite Bridges: Advantages and specific design considerations for
bridges.
Composite Box Girders: Behavior of box girder bridges, design concepts for bending, shear,
and torsion.
Design Procedures: Application of design principles to composite bridge decks and girders.

#### Unit- 6.0 Seismic Behaviour and Case Studies
7 hrs
Seismic Behavior: Performance of composite structures under seismic loading, design
considerations for ductility and energy dissipation.
Fire Engineering: Basic principles of fire design for composite members.
Case Studies: Real-world examples of steel-concrete composite construction in buildings
and bridges, and discussion of their unique design challenges and solutions.

## Advanced Concrete Technology
**Course Code-**

#### Unit- 1.0 Constituent Materials & Chemistry
7 hrs
Cement manufacture, composition, hydration process, and types (OPC, PPC, etc.). Properties
and classification of aggregates (physical, thermal, soundness). Quality of mixing water.

GGBFS) and their effects.

7 hrs
Workability and its measurement (slump, flow tests), rheological behavior, handling, placing,

hardened concrete: strength, elasticity, creep, shrinkage (plastic and drying), and fracture
mechanics.

Mechanisms of degradation: permeability, chemical attack (acid, sulphate, sea water), alkali-
aggregate reaction (AAR), reinforcement corrosion, and freeze-thaw cycles. Strategies for
enhancing durability and performance-based specifications.

7 hrs
Principles of mix design. Detailed procedures for normal and high-performance concrete mix
proportioning using standard methods (e.g., IS Code, ACI method, Road Note No. 4). Quality
control in concrete construction, batching, mixing, and transportation.

7 hrs
Types and applications of various special concretes: High-Strength Concrete (HSC), High-
Performance Concrete (HPC), Self-Compacting Concrete (SCC), Fiber-Reinforced Concrete
(FRC), Lightweight and Heavyweight Concrete, Mass Concrete, Roller-Compacted Concrete
(RCC), and Shotcrete/Gunite. Introduction to novel technologies like 3D printing and
concrete recycling.

Destructive testing methods. Advanced Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) methods for
hardened concrete: rebound hammer, ultrasonic pulse velocity, core tests, pull-out tests,

## Prestressed Concrete
**Course Code-**
Prestressed Concrete
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction and Materials
7 hrs
Basic Concepts: Principles of prestressing; evolution of prestressed concrete; advantages and
limitations compared to reinforced concrete.
Methods of Prestressing: Detailed study of pre-tensioning and post-tensioning methods;
different systems of prestressing (e.g., Hoyer, Magnel, Freyssinet, Gifford-Udall systems);
anchorages and auxiliary equipment.
Materials: Properties of high-strength concrete and high-tensile steel; stress-strain
characteristics; IS/ACI Code provisions for materials.
Construction Techniques Coordination: Overview of the interplay between design
requirements and practical construction techniques in precasting yards and on-site.

#### Unit- 2.0 Analysis of Prestressed Concrete Members
7 hrs
Analysis Methods: Stress concept, force concept, and load balancing methods.
Stress Analysis: Analysis of members under flexure for different stages: initial (at transfer),
service loads, and ultimate loads; permissible stresses in concrete and steel as per codes.
Pressure Line: Concept of the pressure line or C-line and its applications in analysis.
Kern Points: Determination of kern distances for various sections.

#### Unit- 3.0 Losses of Prestress and Deflections
7 hrs
Losses in Prestress: Detailed calculation of instantaneous and time-dependent losses,
including elastic shortening, friction, anchorage slip, creep of concrete, shrinkage of concrete,
and relaxation of steel.
Total Loss: Estimation of the total percentage loss in both pre-tensioned and post-tensioned
members.
Deflections: Factors influencing deflections; short-term and long-term deflections of
uncracked and cracked members due to gravity loads and prestressing force; check for
serviceability limit state of deflection.

#### Unit- 4.0 Design of Flexural and Shear Members
7 hrs
Design for Flexure: Principles of limit state design (ultimate and serviceability) as per IS
1343/ACI Code; design of Type 1 and Type 2 beams; strength evaluations; layout of
cables/tendons in pre-tensioned and post-tensioned beams.
Design for Shear and Torsion: Analysis and design for shear and torsional resistance; codal
provisions for web reinforcement design.
Bond and Anchorage: Transmission length in pre-tensioned members; anchorage zone
stresses in post-tensioned members (Magnel's method, Guyon's method); design of anchorage
zone reinforcement.

#### Unit- 5.0 Precast and Composite Construction
7 hrs
Precast Construction: Specific emphasis on production techniques, handling, transportation,
and erection of precast prestressed elements.
Composite Beams: Analysis and design of composite construction involving precast PSC
beams and cast-in-situ RC slabs; effects of differential creep and shrinkage; methods of
achieving continuity.
Partial Prestressing: Principles, analysis, and design concepts of partial prestressing; crack
width calculations and control.

#### Unit- 6.0 Special Structures and Applications
7 hrs
Statically Indeterminate Structures: Analysis and design of continuous beams and frames;
concept of secondary moments; concordant cable profiles and linear transformation.
Other Applications: Principles of design for special structures such as prestressed concrete
pipes, water tanks, columns, and poles.
Coordination: Final review of the crucial link between design assumptions and actual
construction practices to ensure structural integrity and economy.

## Soil Dynamics and Machine Foundation
**Course Code-**
Soil Dynamics and Machine Foundation
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Fundamentals of Vibration
7 hrs
Introduction: Nature and types of dynamic loading (earthquakes, machine vibrations, blats,
traffic), importance of soil dynamics, and vibration tolerances.
Theory of Vibration: Basic definitions, properties of harmonic motion, degrees of freedom.
Single Degree of Freedom (SDOF) Systems: Free and forced vibrations with and without
viscous damping.
Response Analysis: Frequency-dependent exciting forces, systems under transient forces,
Duhamel's integral, and Rayleigh's method.
Multi-Degree of Freedom Systems: Introduction to two-degree and multi-degree of freedom
systems.

#### Unit- 2.0 Wave Propagation and Dynamic Soil Properties
7 hrs
Wave Propagation Theory: Elastic waves in rods, waves in an infinite, homogeneous, and
isotropic elastic medium, waves in elastic half-space (P-waves, S-waves, Rayleigh waves,
Love waves).
Dynamic Soil Properties: Stress-strain relationships under dynamic loading, shear modulus
(G), elastic modulus (E), damping ratio, and Poisson's ratio.
Determination of Properties: Laboratory methods (resonant column test, cyclic triaxial test,
cyclic direct shear test) and field methods (seismic reflection/refraction, uphole, downhole,
and crosshole methods, cyclic plate load test, block vibration test).

#### Unit- 3.0 Design of Machine Foundations - I (Reciprocating Machines)
7 hrs
Machine Foundations: Types of machines and foundations, general requirements and design
criteria (permissible amplitudes and bearing pressure as per IS codes).
Methods of Analysis: Linear elastic weightless spring method (Barkan's method), elastic
half-space theory, and semi-graphical approaches.
Vibration Analysis: Analysis of vertical, sliding, rocking, and yawing modes of vibration for
a block foundation.
Design Procedures: Detailed design procedures for foundations of reciprocating machines,
calculation of induced forces and moments (as per relevant IS codes like IS 2974).

#### Unit- 4.0 Design of Machine Foundations - II (Impact and Rotary Machines) 7 hrs
Foundations for Impact Machines: Design criteria and dynamic analysis, computation of
dynamic forces, design of hammer foundations (as per IS codes).
Foundations for Rotary Machines: Special design considerations for high-speed rotary
machines like turbines and generators.
Coupled Vibrations: Introduction to simultaneous rocking, sliding, and vertical vibrations.

#### Unit- 5.0 Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering Concepts
7 hrs
Dynamic Earth Pressure: Active and passive earth pressures under dynamic conditions,
design of retaining walls under seismic loads.
Slope Stability: Dynamic slope stability analysis methods.
Soil Liquefaction: Basic concepts and mechanism of liquefaction, factors affecting
susceptibility, evaluation of liquefaction potential (using CPT or SPT data), and mitigation
measures.

#### Unit- 6.0 Vibration Isolation and Advanced Topics
7 hrs
Vibration Isolation: Principles of active and passive vibration isolation, transmissibility
concept, and design of isolation barriers/trenches.
Isolating Materials: Properties and selection of isolating materials.
Pile Foundations: Introduction to dynamic response of single piles and pile groups, one-
dimensional wave equation for pile driving analysis.
Soil-Structure Interaction: Basic concepts of dynamic soil-structure interaction.

7 hrs
Physical characteristics (size, weight, wingspan, length, tail height, wheel base, gear tread,
engine type) and how they influence airport design (runway length/width, taxiway geometry,
apron/hanger size, pavement strength, noise, jet blast). Performance characteristics include
speed (cruising, air, landing, take-off), payload/range, take-off distance required, climb rate,
and the impact of atmospheric conditions (temperature, pressure, wind) and field elevation on
performance.

#### Unit- 2.0 Airport Planning and Demand Forecasting
7 hrs
Airport Master Plan process (short & long-range planning); demand forecasting for
passenger, cargo, and aircraft movements; site selection factors (regional plan, ground
accessibility, topography, obstructions, meteorological conditions like wind and visibility,
environmental impact, economic considerations).

#### Unit- 3.0 Geometric Design of the Airfield
7 hrs
Runway design (orientation, wind rose diagram analysis, geometric standards, length
requirements, capacity and configuration); taxiway design (geometric standards, fillets, high-
speed exit taxiways); apron design (holding and terminal aprons, gate positions, parking
systems).

#### Unit- 4.0 Airside and Landside Infrastructure
7 hrs
Airside infrastructure (airport drainage, airfield lighting systems, markings, safety areas);
landside planning (terminal building function and design, passenger flow, space planning,
ground access systems, parking, road networks).

#### Unit- 5.0 Terminal Design and Capacity Analysis
7 hrs
Design of passenger and cargo terminals; terminal philosophies; capacity analysis for airside
and terminal facilities; delay and congestion management; use of simulation tools; capacity of
runways, taxiways, and gates.

#### Unit- 6.0 Air Traffic Management and Navigational Aids
7 hrs
Air traffic control and surveillance facilities; navigational aids (ground-based systems like
Instrument Landing Systems (ILS), VOR, DME; satellite-based systems like GPS, RNAV);
communication systems; aviation regulatory bodies (ICAO, FAA) and safety standards.
Text/ Reference:-

## Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
**Course Code-**
Solid and Hazardous Waste Management
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Solid Wastes: Origin, Analysis, Composition, and Characteristics
7 hrs
Introduction: Definition of solid waste, types (domestic, commercial, institutional,
industrial, agricultural, etc.), and need for management.
Sources and Generation: Origin of solid wastes from various human and animal activities,
factors affecting waste generation rates, and quantification.
Analysis and Composition: Physical (moisture content, density, particle size), chemical
(proximate analysis, calorific value, nutrient content), and biological properties.
Characteristics: Identification of hazardous content and degradability, and public health and
ecological impacts.

#### Unit- 2.0 Integrated Solid Waste Management System (ISWMS) - Functional Elements
7 hrs
ISWMS Concept: Principles and hierarchy (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover, Dispose),
and role of stakeholders.
Storage and Collection: On-site storage methods, types of containers, collection systems,
and collection routes optimization.
Segregation, Reuse, and Recycling: Importance of source segregation, material recovery
potential, and setting up recycling units.
Transfer and Transportation: Need for transfer stations, and methods for efficient
transportation.

#### Unit- 3.0 Treatment / Processing and Transformation Techniques, and Final Disposal
7 hrs
Processing Techniques: Objectives of waste processing, material separation technologies.
Biological Treatment: Composting (aerobic and anaerobic), vermicomposting, and their
design and operation.
Thermal Treatment: Incineration with energy recovery, pyrolysis, and gasification.
Final Disposal: Landfilling concepts, site selection criteria, design and operation of sanitary
landfills, secure landfills, and landfill bioreactors.
Landfill Management: Leachate and landfill gas management, closure, and post-closure
monitoring.

#### Unit- 4.0 Management of Specific Solid Wastes and Legislation
7 hrs
Municipal Solid Wastes (MSW): Management practices and salient features of relevant
rules and regulations (e.g., Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 in India).
Biomedical Wastes: Characterization, handling, treatment, and disposal methods, including
relevant rules (e.g., Biomedical Waste Management Rules).
Electronic Wastes (E-waste): Magnitude of the problem, management, and relevant
regulations.
Industrial Solid Wastes: Specific challenges and management practices.
Nuclear/Radioactive Wastes: Introduction to nuclear waste management and regulations.

#### Unit- 5.0 Introduction to Hazardous Wastes, Risk Assessment, and Minimization
7 hrs
Introduction and Definition: Definition of hazardous waste, magnitude of the problem, and
hazardous characteristics (ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity).
Legislation and Characterization: Environmental legislation, characterization methods
(e.g., TCLP tests), and site assessment.
Risk Assessment: Quantitative risk assessment and health/environmental considerations.
Waste Minimization and Resource Recovery: Techniques for source reduction, waste
exchange, and resource recovery.
Transportation: Storage, labeling, handling, manifests, and transport protocols.

#### Unit- 6.0 Hazardous Waste Treatment, Disposal, and Site Remediation
7 hrs
Treatment Technologies: Physical (solidification/stabilization, filtration, etc.), chemical
(neutralization,
oxidation/reduction,
precipitation),
and
biological
treatments
(bioremediation).
Disposal: Secure landfills design and operation.
Environmental Monitoring and Auditing: Ground water contamination issues,

Facility Development and Operation: Siting criteria (NIMBY, LULU concepts), and

## Water Resource Management
**Course Code-**
Water Resource Management
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction to Water Resources and Management
7 hrs
Concepts and Significance: Definition of water resources management (WRM), global and
Indian water scenarios (surface and groundwater), water scarcity, stress, and security.
The Hydrologic Cycle and Budget: Review of the hydrological cycle and water balance
equation.
Planning and Management Approaches: Need for planning, top-down vs. bottom-up
approaches, principles and pillars of Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM).
Water Use: Water withdrawal and consumption by sector (domestic, agriculture, industry),
water footprint concepts.

#### Unit- 2.0 Hydrological Processes and Assessment
7 hrs
Precipitation and Abstractions: Types and measurement of precipitation, water losses
(evaporation, evapotranspiration, infiltration), and estimation methods.
Runoff and Streamflow: Runoff components and factors affecting them, hydrograph
analysis, unit hydrograph theory, rainfall-runoff models.
Groundwater Hydrology: Origin and occurrence of groundwater, properties of aquifers,
Darcy's law, groundwater flow, and assessment methods (well hydraulics, safe yield).

#### Unit- 3.0 Water Quality and Environmental Aspects
7 hrs
Water Quality Parameters: Physical, chemical (e.g., pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen),
and biological parameters, water quality indices.
Water Pollution: Sources and types of pollution (point and non-point), impact on water
resources and ecosystems.
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): Principles and methodologies for assessing the
environmental impact of water resource projects.

#### Unit- 4.0 Water Resource Systems Planning and Engineering
7 hrs
Project Planning and Analysis: Objectives of water resources planning and development,
data needs, project analysis, and economic evaluation techniques (Benefit-Cost Analysis,
discounting).
Water Infrastructure: Planning and design of key components like reservoirs, irrigation
systems (canals, headworks), and water distribution networks.
Systems Analysis and Modeling: Introduction to systems concepts, optimization techniques
(linear and dynamic programming), and simulation models for water resource systems.

#### Unit- 5.0 Water Resource Management in Practice
7 hrs
Irrigation Water Management: Need for irrigation, soil-water-plant relationships, irrigation
scheduling, and water use efficiency.
Watershed Management: Concept and principles of watershed management, soil and water
conservation practices (e.g., contour bunding, rainwater harvesting, farm ponds).
Flood and Drought Management: Design flood estimation, flood routing, flood mitigation
strategies, and drought planning.

#### Unit- 6.0 Water Governance, Policy, and Climate Change
7 hrs
Water Governance and Policy: Elements of effective water governance, National Water
Policies, legal aspects, and inter-state water conflicts in India.
Socio-Economic Aspects: Valuing water (use and non-use values), water economics, and
pricing models.
Climate Change and Sustainability: Impact of climate change on water availability,
sustainable water resource planning and management under climate uncertainty.
Modern Tools: Application of GIS, remote sensing, and modeling software in water
resources management.

## Hydraulic modelling
**Course Code-**
Hydraulic modelling
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction and Fundamental Principles
7 hrs
Concepts of Modeling: Philosophy and concepts, types of hydraulic modeling (physical and
mathematical/numerical).
Theoretical Background: Review of basic fluid mechanics and hydraulics principles (e.g.,
continuity, momentum, and energy equations).
Dimensional Analysis and Similitude: Laws of similitude, model scales, Froude, Reynolds,
and Weber number applications, and limitations of physical models.

#### Unit- 2.0 Open Channel Flow Modeling
7 hrs
Governing Equations: Derivation of unsteady and steady flow equations (Saint-Venant
equations, 1D/2D RANS).
Flow Regimes: Detailed treatment of subcritical, supercritical, and transcritical flows.
Numerical Methods: Introduction to finite difference and finite volume methods for solving
open channel flow problems.
Applications: Flood routing in channels and rivers, dam break flood wave analysis.

#### Unit- 3.0 Closed Conduit (Pipe) Flow Modeling
7 hrs
Hydraulic Principles: Head losses (major and minor) in pipes, Darcy-Weisbach equation,
pipes in series and parallel.
Network Analysis: Analysis of water distribution networks, loop and path head loss
methods, and network components.
Software Tools: Introduction to and application of industry-standard software tools (e.g.,
EPANET).
Transient Flow: Introduction to water hammer and surge analysis.

#### Unit- 4.0 Physical Hydraulic Models
7 hrs
Development and Construction: Procedures and tools for developing physical models of
hydraulic structures.
Model Testing: Instrumentation for testing and data collection in physical models.
Applications: Modeling of spillways, energy dissipators, culverts, and other hydraulic
structures.

#### Unit- 5.0 Computational Hydraulic Modeling (Software Focus)
7 hrs
Software Applications: Practical application of advanced software for river, urban drainage,
and coastal modeling (e.g., HEC-RAS, SWMM, MIKE software).
Data Handling: Use of GIS (Geographic Information Systems) and Remote Sensing for data
input, model setup, and result visualization.
Model Calibration and Validation: Procedures for calibrating and validating numerical
models using field data.

#### Unit- 6.0 Environmental and Specialized Modeling
7 hrs
Sediment Transport: Introduction to movable bed models and sediment transport in shallow
water systems.
Environmental Aspects: Modeling of water quality, pollutant transport, and environmental
impact assessment.
Advanced Topics: Overview of groundwater modeling, estuarine, and coastal hydraulics
modeling.

## Port Harbor Engineering
**Course Code-**
Port Harbor Engineering
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Introduction to Ports and Harbours & Natural Phenomena
7 hrs
Introduction: History of ports, advantages and modern trends of water transportation,
definitions of port and harbour, functions and classification of harbours (e.g., natural,
artificial, commercial, fishing).
Site Selection & Planning: Factors affecting site selection, characteristics of a good harbour,
ship characteristics, port authorities, and general layout of port works.
Natural Phenomena: Understanding tides, wind, water waves, and currents; their
characteristics and effects on marine structures; littoral drift; and the use of the wind rose
diagram.

#### Unit- 2.0 Harbour Fundamentals and Design Issues
7 hrs
Wave Hydrodynamics: Wave conditions inside the harbour, water circulation, wave
reflection, design wave characteristics, and return periods.
Design Issues: Sea port layout considerations regarding wave action, siltation, and
navigability.
Port Planning: National policies, design principles, cargo volume forecasts, port
productivity, and planning of specific terminals (general cargo, container, marinas, fishing
ports).

#### Unit- 3.0 Marine Structures I: Breakwaters and Berthing Structures
7 hrs
Breakwaters: Function, types (mound, wall, composite), general design principles, and
construction methods.
Berthing Structures: Types of berthing structures (wharves, quays, jetties, piers, pier heads,
dolphins), loads on berthing structures (berthing force, mooring force, seismic force), and
design principles.
Fenders and Mooring: Types of fenders (wooden, rubber, etc.), mooring accessories, and
design of mooring systems.

#### Unit- 4.0 Marine Structures II: Docks and Repair Facilities
7 hrs
Docks: Necessity of docks, distinction between harbour dock and tidal basin, types of docks
(wet docks, dry docks, graving docks, floating docks).
Repair Facilities: Slipways, ship lifts, and general maintenance and renovation aspects of
ports and inland waterways.
Geotechnical Aspects: Foundation design of piles, pile load tests, ground improvement
techniques, and active/passive earth pressure considerations.

#### Unit- 5.0 Port Facilities and Operations
7 hrs
Cargo Handling: Cargo handling equipment, bulk material storage and handling, and
planning of multipurpose port terminals.
Support Facilities: Port building facilities, transit sheds, warehouses, and other ancillary
services.
Navigation and Traffic: Navigational channels design, ship characteristics in channels,
navigational aids (fixed and floating), Vessel Traffic Management Systems (VTMS), and
traffic forecasts.

#### Unit- 6.0 Dredging, Coastal Protection, and Environmental Aspects
7 hrs
Dredging: General principles, classification of dredging works, types of dredgers and
equipment, disposal of dredged material (including contaminated sediments), and cost
estimation.
Coastal Protection: Design of coastal protection works like sea walls, revetments, and
bulkheads.
Environmental Impact: Environmental impact assessments (EIA), construction of
environmentally engineered banks, and considerations for climate change and sea-level rise.

## RS and GIS Application in Civil Engineering
**Course Code-**
RS and GIS Application in Civil Engineering
3 0 0 3

#### Unit- 1.0 Fundamentals of Remote Sensing
7 hrs
Basic concepts, elements involved (energy source, atmosphere, ground features, sensors,
platforms). Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS), atmospheric windows, energy interactions
with atmosphere and earth surface features (vegetation, water, soil). Resolutions: spatial,
spectral, radiometric, and temporal.

#### Unit- 2.0 Data Acquisition and Interpretation
7 hrs
Types of platforms (airborne, spaceborne) and sensors (optical, thermal, microwave). Data
products and formats. Principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry (types of
photographs, scale, stereoscopy, parallax measurement). Visual interpretation techniques and
keys.

#### Unit- 3.0 Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Principles
7 hrs
Introduction to GIS, definitions, components (hardware, software, data, users, procedures).
Spatial and non-spatial (attribute) data. Types of maps, map projections, and coordinate
systems. Raster and vector data structures, advantages and disadvantages.

#### Unit- 4.0 GIS Data Input, Analysis, and Output
7 hrs
Data input methods (digitizing, scanning, GPS data). Data editing and topology creation.
Spatial analysis methods (retrieval, reclassification, overlay analysis, buffering). Data output
(printers, plotters, digital formats). Introduction to Global Positioning System (GPS)
fundamentals.

#### Unit- 5.0 Digital Image Processing (DIP)
7 hrs
Principles of DIP, pre-processing (radiometric and geometric corrections, image registration).
Image enhancement techniques (contrast manipulation, filtering). Image classification
(supervised, unsupervised, hybrid) and accuracy assessment.

#### Unit- 6.0 Applications in Civil Engineering
7 hrs
Specific applications in: Water Resources (watershed management, flood monitoring,
groundwater assessment, irrigation management), Urban Planning (land use/land cover
mapping, site selection, urban sprawl analysis), Transportation (route alignment, traffic
management), and Disaster Management (drought assessment, environmental impact
analysis).
Text/ Reference:-
1. "Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation" by T.M. Lillesand and R.W. Kiefer.
2. "An Introduction to Geographical Information Systems" by I. Heywood, S. Cornelius,
and S. Carver.
3. Additional suggested textbooks include "Remote Sensing and GIS: Principles &
Applications" by Dr. Basavaraja Simpi, et al. and "Geomatics Engineering" by Prof.
Surbhi Jain and Prof. Mukesh Rai.
4. "Remote Sensing - Principles and Interpretation" by F.F. Sabins Jr..
5. Other reference books include "Principles of Remote Sensing" by Paul J. Gibson and
"Fundamentals of Satellite Remote Sensing" by Arthur Cracknell and Alun Vaughan.
